extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (practitioners of patent contract and equity law)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing the rights, wrongs, and remedies between parties to patent-related contracts (assignments, grants, licenses), including when equity will order specific performance, rescission, damages, or injunctive relief. Focused on U.S. patent practice and common-law equitable doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment vs. License (nature of conveyance)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment or grant conveys the whole or part of the monopoly and creates a property interest in the transferee; a license conveys nothing and is a simple agreement not to enforce the patent privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments are governed by the same rules as sales of personal or real estate (warranty, fraud, failure of consideration, etc.). Licenses create different obligations, estoppels, and defenses; every user may either practice at the risk of suit or pay the license fee and be exempt. (Text and cases cited: Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement contrary to contractual terms is a breach of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contracting party infringes the patent contrary to the terms of an agreement with the owner, that infringement is also a violation of the covenant (i.e., a breach of contract) and may give rise to contract remedies in addition to tort remedies for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same person may be liable both as a contracting party (for breach) and as a stranger (for tort); plaintiff may pursue either contract or tort remedies. (See discussion at §1225 and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee's contract rights and categories of assignor wrongs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under his contract, an assignee is entitled to a perfect legal title to a valid patent, without fraud or imposition, and with fulfillment of express and implied warranties. Violations include: (1) refusal to convey; (2) conveyance of defective title; (3) conveyance of an invalid patent; (4) deceit or artifice inducing the transaction; (5) breach of warranty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each listed wrong an adequate remedy exists in law or equity. The treatise enumerates these categories expressly (§1227) so they should be treated as distinct bases for relief and analyzed separately in any dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy when assignor refuses to convey (voluntary vs involuntary refusal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the assignor's neglect/refusal to convey is involuntary, the assignee's remedy is an action at law for breach of contract; if voluntary, the assignee may sue for damages or obtain specific performance in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will compel performance of assignment contracts where necessary to prevent irreparable injury; oral contracts to convey a future patent may be enforced after grant. But relief depends on equitable principles (see cases Adams v. Messinger, Somerby v. Buntin, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on specific performance of patent assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific performance of a contract to assign a patent will not be decreed when performance would be inequitable, contrary to public policy, futile or afford imperfect relief, when the plaintiff has been guilty of laches (unless defendant acquiesced), when performance would require supervision of personal services/skill/judgment, or where the exact thing to be done cannot be described or would disclose secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: equity will refuse performance where prior assignments or expiration make decree ineffective; will not decree performance of personal skilled services (Wollensak v. Briggs); will refuse unconscionable bargains (Pope Mfg. Co. v. Gormully). Also if bona fide purchasers' rights have intervened, specific performance may be denied. Cases and nuanced rules are cited throughout (§1228 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction as an equitable alternative to specific performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct specific performance is unavailable or impracticable, equity may enjoin the assignor from transferring or enjoying the patent contrary to the assignee's rights, effectively coercing compliance with the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may forbid transfer or sale to third parties (injunction) to protect the assignee's equitable interest; injunctions are used where they will do substantial justice between the parties even if the court cannot directly supervise manufacture or performance. (See Singer Mfg. Co. v. Union Button Hole & Embroidery Co. and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when title proves defective after conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: If title proves defective after completion and the assignee has performed, equity may compel the assignor to perfect title if possible; if not, the assignee may rescind and be restored or seek damages at law. Partial defects that cannot be adequately compensated justify rescission; on rescission the assignee must reconvey and account for benefits received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When consideration was a specific sum already paid and title wholly fails, the assignee may recover the price after tender of the patent. Measure of damages is the loss caused by defective title. Cases and examples provided (§1229 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent invalidity on the assignment (no consideration / failure of consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conveyance of an invalid patent forms no consideration for a contract; an assignee who in good faith and with due caution relied on its validity is entitled upon discovery to a return of property or release from obligations. The ground of invalidity (novelty, utility, priority) is immaterial for this principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include rescission or money recovery; assignee who had means to discover the defect or who accepted obvious defects cannot complain (caveat emptor). If the defect is curable by the assignor, the assignee generally must accept perfection rather than rescind. (See §1230 and supporting notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Uselessness, defect of specification, and other grounds affecting consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent is void because the invention is useless or the specification defective, there is a failure of consideration; notes and cases show that money paid for a void patent can be recovered, with various limits depending on knowledge and benefits received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules: a note given for a patent void for uselessness is void (Rowe v. Blanchard); buyer who knew all facts cannot recover; if buyer accepted and derived benefits, recovery may be limited and accounting required; improvements that make invention useful may affect relief. (Detailed examples and citations in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conveyance of different invention equals invalid patent; acceptance estops rescission
rubrics_metrics.description: A conveyance of a patent covering a different invention than agreed is equivalent to conveyance of an invalid patent; the assignee may rescind or recover price, but if the assignee accepts the conveyance and avails himself of the invention's advantages, he is estopped from later claiming breach or invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee's conduct after conveyance (acceptance, enjoying benefits) is crucial to availability of rescission; equity will require reconveyance and accounting when rescission is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent procurement of assignment (rescission and damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the assignor induced the assignee by deceit or artifice, the assignment may be set aside in equity or the assignee may recover damages at law. Fraud may consist of false statements of existing fact, exhibition of false devices, or other deliberate misrepresentations intended to induce purchase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish opinion from fact: mere optimistic statements of value are usually non-fraudulent; willful falsehoods about validity, novelty, utility, salability, or coverage of the patent, if intended to deceive and acted upon, are fraud. Representations by agents bind the assignor. Remedies require prompt action after discovery and often an offer to return benefits; if the assignee has exercised ownership and enjoyed benefits after discovery, rescission is barred though damages may still lie. (Extensive cases and nuance in §1231.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyer’s knowledge and the doctrine of caveat emptor
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability of the assignee to have discovered the truth (e.g., by searching Patent Office records or consulting skilled persons) does not necessarily bar relief if the vendor intentionally deceived; however, if both parties had equal knowledge or means of knowledge and acted in good faith, equity will not relieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If purchaser had full knowledge before paying, recovery is often barred; but corporate purchasers may have special exceptions (see next criterion). Promptness in seeking rescission after discovery is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate purchaser exception to caveat emptor
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation purchasing rights to sell an invention may rely on the vendors' representations and is not always bound by caveat emptor; it may sue for fraudulent representations made to persons who formed the corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations may recover for fraudulent inducement even where a sole buyer might be subject to caveat emptor; cases cited include Iowa Economic Heater Co. v. American Economic Heater Co. and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee holding patent with notice of prior unrecorded assignment holds in trust
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee who, before obtaining the patent, has notice of a prior unrecorded assignment and nevertheless procures the patent to himself holds it in trust for the prior assignee and may be compelled to assign to that prior assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable conversion and trust principles apply; courts will order conveyance to the true owner where notice existed. (See §1228 notes and cited cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Election of remedies and inability to both enforce and rescind
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee cannot simultaneously claim both enforcement and rescission for the same defect; he must elect between rescissory relief and enforcement remedies (though damages may be sought in some circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the defective title can be made perfect by assignor's acts, courts generally require the assignee to accept perfection rather than rescind. If an assignee seeks rescission he must account for benefits received; if he seeks enforcement he cannot also recover rescissory relief for the same conduct. (Citations in §1229–§1230.)
